title: Benchmark governance: High scores may lack workplace meaning
desc: Separates technical quality, reproducibility and real-world suitability while examining contamination, incentives and representation.

kps.k: Benchmark quality and real-world suitability are separate questions; a high score does not by itself establish reliable professional performance.
kps.d: The cluster’s substantive argument concerns the limits of benchmark-based assurance, rather than whether AI capabilities exist. Eriksson and colleagues’ interdisciplinary review links measurement validity to deployment context, while BetterBench distinguishes what a benchmark measures from how people use its results. BetterBench explicitly limits its framework to minimum quality assurance, not validation for a particular application. The supplied material therefore supports scrutiny of the inference from test scores to practical reliability, not a conclusion that benchmarks are useless.

qs.q: 2         Related Work 2.1        AI Benchmarking Practices and Challenges  Our literature review of AI benchmarking practices identifies two primary concerns: what a bench- mark measures and how this measurement is used.
qs.a: BetterBench: Assessing AI Benchmarks, Uncovering Issues, and Establishing Best Practices · Academia · 2024

qs.q: Aside from mainly focusing on a small range of tasks, previous research has identified that most benchmarks tend to be abstracted out of their social and cultural context [Selbst et al., 2019; Lum et al., 2024], are aggregated in problematic ways [Burnell et al., 2023], and rely on a static, one-time testing logic, where results from single evaluations are taken to represent model capabilities writ large.
qs.a: Can We Trust AI Benchmarks? An Interdisciplinary Review of Current Issues in AI Evaluation · Regulators & courts · 2025

kps.k: The strongest direct evidence concerns benchmark design and reproducibility, not measured workplace outcomes.
kps.d: BetterBench develops 46 lifecycle criteria from literature and expert interviews and applies them to 24 benchmarks, including 16 foundation-model and eight non-foundation-model benchmarks. It finds substantial quality differences and reports that most do not provide statistical significance or easy replication. Eriksson and colleagues synthesise around 110 publications from 2014–2024 using snowball sampling, rather than conducting new model tests or a systematic database search. Their discussion of Reuel and colleagues’ assessment overlaps with BetterBench and should not count as independent corroboration.

qs.q: In this paper, we develop an assessment framework considering 46                                                       best practices across an AI benchmark’s lifecycle and evaluate 24 AI benchmarks                                                       against it.
qs.a: BetterBench: Assessing AI Benchmarks, Uncovering Issues, and Establishing Best Practices · Academia · 2024

qs.q: To achieve this, we gather and analyse around 110 publications published between 1st January 2014 and 31st December 2024 that explicitly and primarily address limitations in current benchmarking practices.
qs.a: Can We Trust AI Benchmarks? An Interdisciplinary Review of Current Issues in AI Evaluation · Regulators & courts · 2025

kps.k: Several distinct mechanisms can make benchmark scores misleading.
kps.d: The interdisciplinary review separates shortcut learning, training-data contamination, implementation sensitivity and restricted audit access. It reports a medical-imaging example in which a collapsed-lung classifier relied on chest drains rather than the intended diagnostic feature, with performance falling by over 20% after drain-containing images were removed. It also reports studies showing that models can be programmed to underperform and that safety scores can correlate strongly with upstream capabilities. These findings raise different interpretive problems: apparent capability may reflect shortcuts, concealed capability may evade tests, and apparent safety improvement may reflect general capability gains. They do not establish that every benchmark exhibits these failures.

qs.q: [2019] found that an X-ray image classification model predicted collapsed lungs with high accuracy, although it turned out the model only identified the presence of a chest drain (used to cure the condition) that was (unknowingly) present in a majority of the positive training images.
qs.a: Can We Trust AI Benchmarks? An Interdisciplinary Review of Current Issues in AI Evaluation · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: When the all images containing chest drains were removed from the training dataset, the model performance dropped by over 20%.
qs.a: Can We Trust AI Benchmarks? An Interdisciplinary Review of Current Issues in AI Evaluation · Regulators & courts · 2025

kps.k: Evaluation must account for interaction, failure modes and change over time, not only isolated task success.
kps.d: Eriksson and colleagues report calls for repeated, longitudinal and multilayered evaluation because one-time tests can miss within-model variation, human behaviour and risks from interacting systems. TheAgentCompany supplies a useful distinction between tool interfaces, occupational coverage, intermediate checkpoint scoring and interaction with NPC agents; its supplied excerpts provide no success rates or evidence of collaboration benefits. PRBench similarly presents public release as a research step toward reliable decision support, not proof that systems can replace professionals.

qs.q: This has given rise to calls for more multi-layered [Weidinger et al., 2023], longitudinal [Mizrahi et al., 2024], and holistic evaluation methods that can be reproduced [Kapoor et al., 2024], and prove that AI models do not just perform well in controlled environments, but also in critical/real-world circumstances over time [Ojewale et al., 2024; McIntosh et al., 2024; Chang et al., 2023].
qs.a: Can We Trust AI Benchmarks? An Interdisciplinary Review of Current Issues in AI Evaluation · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: Long-Horizon with Checkpoints: if tasks are evaluated at intermediate checkpoints and assigned partial scores.
qs.a: TheAgentCompany: Benchmarking LLM Agents on Consequential Real World Tasks · Academia · 2024

kps.k: Benchmark governance involves institutional incentives and representation as well as technical quality.
kps.d: The interdisciplinary review argues that benchmarks shape training and deployment while commercial competition encourages score optimisation over explanation. It reports concentrated institutional influence, English-dominated safety evaluation and minority under-representation. BetterBench adds a qualification to reform: demanding domain-expert involvement and other quality practices may disadvantage less-resourced researchers and narrow participation. The resulting tension concerns how to improve assurance without reinforcing the resource concentration that the review criticises.

qs.q: This happens as benchmarks continuously influence how AI models are trained, fine-tuned, and applied - practices with wide-ranging political, economic, and cultural effects.
qs.a: Can We Trust AI Benchmarks? An Interdisciplinary Review of Current Issues in AI Evaluation · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: The issue of optimising for high benchmark scores at the expense of insight and explanation is known as a form of SOTA-chasing [Koch et al., 2021] and sometimes described as the "benchmark effect" [Stewart, 2023].
qs.a: Can We Trust AI Benchmarks? An Interdisciplinary Review of Current Issues in AI Evaluation · Regulators & courts · 2025

kps.k: The practical response is qualified, lifecycle-based assurance rather than a universal benchmark.
kps.d: Eriksson and colleagues recommend standardised methods for assessing benchmark trustworthiness, not necessarily uniform metrics or tests. BetterBench translates this approach into a checklist, living assessment repository, maintenance and retirement practices. It recommends replacing saturated or irrelevant tests, communicating transitions and archiving materials. NIST’s supplied draft excerpt adds that reports should explain agreement and disagreement with comparable evaluations and other evidence. These proposals address growing regulatory reliance, but neither BetterBench nor the review demonstrates that adoption will reduce downstream harm; mitigation effectiveness and uptake remain uncertain.

qs.q: But we do need standardised methods for assessing the trustworthiness of benchmarks from an applied and regulatory perspective.
qs.a: Can We Trust AI Benchmarks? An Interdisciplinary Review of Current Issues in AI Evaluation · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: Once the benchmark and its documentation are released, developers must conduct regular maintenance to ensure ongoing usability.
qs.a: BetterBench: Assessing AI Benchmarks, Uncovering Issues, and Establishing Best Practices · Academia · 2024

kps.k: The supplied evidence establishes methodological tensions, but not comparative verdicts on legal AI, automated judges or productivity.
kps.d: Most remaining summaries contain bibliographies rather than authorial findings. They cannot establish legal-tool hallucination rates, bar-exam performance, workplace productivity effects, human–AI complementarity or the superiority of rubric, preference or automated evaluation. The substantive sources largely complement rather than contradict one another: BetterBench offers an operational quality framework, the interdisciplinary review stresses broader unresolved limitations, and NIST recommends comparison with other evidence. The review retains qualified confidence that AI safety assurance can develop. The central unresolved issue is how much assurance improved evaluation practices can provide, not an evidenced split between rejecting benchmarks and trusting them unconditionally.

qs.q: There is no reason to believe that similar safety assurances can not be developed for AI, and the intensified interest in AI benchmarks signals a drive to do so.
qs.a: Can We Trust AI Benchmarks? An Interdisciplinary Review of Current Issues in AI Evaluation · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: It is important to recognize that some issues that AI benchmarks seek to address are impossible or extremely difficult to fully address.
qs.a: Can We Trust AI Benchmarks? An Interdisciplinary Review of Current Issues in AI Evaluation · Regulators & courts · 2025

vlens.an: The usable academia-and-research evidence accepts the proposition that benchmark quality is distinct from real-world professional suitability and materially develops it. BetterBench contributes the strongest extension: a 46-practice lifecycle framework, an assessment of 24 benchmarks, evidence of substantial quality and reproducibility weaknesses, and concrete practices for maintenance and retirement. It also expressly limits these measures to minimum quality assurance rather than application-specific validation. TheAgentCompany adds a narrower but complementary contribution by distinguishing occupational coverage, interfaces, intermediate checkpoint scoring and interaction—features relevant to evaluating long-horizon workplace agents rather than isolated end-state success. There is material variation in emphasis: BetterBench focuses on benchmark governance and reproducibility, while TheAgentCompany focuses on task structure and interaction. BetterBench also warns that demanding quality requirements such as domain-expert involvement may disadvantage less-resourced researchers. Most other records are bibliographic or fragmentary and therefore remain unclear; this lack of recoverable evidence is not opposition. Given that this is a curated selection, these findings should not be generalized to academia and research as a whole.

qs.q: However, there is a potential risk of misinterpretation of our results; our assessment only provides minimum quality assurances and is not sufficient to assess the suitability of a benchmark for a concrete use case.
qs.a: BetterBench: Assessing AI Benchmarks, Uncovering Issues, and Establishing Best Practices · Academia · 2024

qs.q: Long-Horizon with Checkpoints: if tasks are evaluated at intermediate checkpoints and assigned partial scores.

vlens.an: The curated regulators, courts and professional-bodies sources collectively build on the proposition that high benchmark scores do not by themselves establish reliable professional or workplace performance. The substantive common ground is that benchmark evidence requires contextualisation and stronger assurance: NIST recommends comparing results with similar evaluations, other evidence and existing knowledge, while the interdisciplinary review explains why isolated scores may mislead through construct-validity problems, contamination, implementation sensitivity, limited reproducibility, static testing, weak representation and incentives to optimise scores. The review materially extends the proposition into governance by advocating standardised methods for assessing benchmark trustworthiness from applied and regulatory perspectives, rather than either abandoning benchmarks or imposing universal tests. Internal variation is material but not contradictory: NIST offers a narrow reporting recommendation and does not address workplace outcomes; the review supplies the broader sociotechnical diagnosis and governance proposal while retaining qualified confidence that safety assurance can improve; and the statistical-toolbox excerpt is bibliographic only, so no position can safely be attributed to it. These sources establish methodological and regulatory concerns, not direct evidence of legal-AI workplace performance or proof that proposed reforms reduce downstream harm.

qs.q: This has given rise to calls for more multi-layered [Weidinger et al., 2023], longitudinal [Mizrahi et al., 2024], and holistic evaluation methods that can be reproduced [Kapoor et al., 2024], and prove that AI models do not just perform well in controlled environments, but also in critical/real-world circumstances over time [Ojewale et al., 2024; McIntosh et al., 2024; Chang et al., 2023].
qs.a: Can We Trust AI Benchmarks? An Interdisciplinary Review of Current Issues in AI Evaluation · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: But we do need standardised methods for assessing the trustworthiness of benchmarks from an applied and regulatory perspective.
qs.a: Can We Trust AI Benchmarks? An Interdisciplinary Review of Current Issues in AI Evaluation · Regulators & courts · 2025

vlens.an: The attributable legal-tech-vendor evidence supports the proposition, but only narrowly. PRBench treats public benchmarking as a research mechanism for advancing transparent and reliable real-world decision support, rather than as evidence that a high benchmark score already demonstrates workplace suitability. This aligns with the cluster’s distinction between benchmark performance and validated professional reliability. Material internal variation is mainly evidentiary rather than substantive: the supplied JudgmentBench, LeMAJ, ATLAS, GDPval, Xpertbench and agentic-governance excerpts are bibliographic material and therefore reveal no authorial position. Their references touch on construct alignment, reproducibility, human grounding, expert tasks and evaluation methods, but cited titles cannot be treated as those sources’ findings or endorsements. Accordingly, the curated vendor evidence offers limited support and no evidenced opposition, but it does not establish a shared vendor view or materially address the cluster’s broader governance concerns about contamination, incentives, representation and lifecycle assurance.

qs.q: By making this benchmark publicly available, we aim to advance research toward transparent, reliable, and economically valuable AI systems capable of assisting in real-world decision-making.
qs.a: PRBench: Large-Scale Expert Rubrics for Evaluating High-Stakes Professional Reasoning · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

elens.an: The 2015–2022 material cannot be positioned relative to the proposition that high benchmark scores may lack workplace meaning. The supplied record contains only bibliographic entries and an incomplete appendix opening, with no substantive claims, findings, predictions or recommendations from the source itself. Titles of cited works are insufficient to infer whether the source supports, extends, redirects or opposes the proposition. Accordingly, this record provides no evidence of either agreement or disagreement, and no broader inference about sources from this period is warranted from this curated item.

The substantive 2023–2024 evidence accepts the proposition that benchmark performance and workplace suitability are distinct, and materially develops it rather than merely restating it. BetterBench contributes the strongest extension: a 46-practice lifecycle framework applied to 24 benchmarks, evidence of quality and reproducibility weaknesses, and concrete practices for maintenance and retirement, while expressly limiting its assessment to minimum quality assurance rather than application-specific validation. TheAgentCompany adds a narrower design contribution by separating occupational coverage, tool interfaces, intermediate checkpoint scoring and interaction—features relevant to evaluating long-horizon agentic work—but the supplied excerpts report no performance outcomes or workplace reliability. Material internal variation therefore concerns scope and evidential strength: BetterBench offers an operational framework and empirical benchmark assessment; TheAgentCompany supplies evaluation dimensions only; and the contamination example in the legal-AI bibliography is a cited commentator’s inference, not a source-level finding. Most other records are bibliographic fragments, so their positions are indeterminate and cannot be treated as corroboration or disagreement. Given this curated evidence, the period builds on the cluster mainly through lifecycle governance and context-sensitive benchmark design, without establishing comparative legal-AI performance or measured workplace outcomes.

elens.an: The attributable 2025 evidence builds on the proposition, although the basis is narrow because most supplied records contain only bibliographies or fragments and are therefore indeterminate. The principal substantive source, Eriksson and colleagues’ interdisciplinary review, accepts that benchmark success does not establish durable real-world reliability and materially develops the proposition by identifying technical, sociotechnical and institutional causes: static testing, contamination, shortcut learning, implementation sensitivity, weak reproducibility, score-optimising incentives and limited representation. It then proposes standardised assessment of benchmark trustworthiness rather than either abandoning benchmarks or imposing universal tests. PRBench is directionally supportive but more limited: it presents public benchmarking as a research step toward reliable real-world decision support, not evidence that present systems are professionally suitable. Internal variation therefore concerns emphasis and evidential strength—not a demonstrated disagreement: the review supplies a broad critique and governance response, PRBench states an enabling aspiration, and the remaining sources cannot be positioned from the excerpts provided. No attributable source in this curated set opposes the proposition, but the indeterminate records should not be treated as support or as evidence of prevalence.

qs.q: This has given rise to calls for more multi-layered [Weidinger et al., 2023], longitudinal [Mizrahi et al., 2024], and holistic evaluation methods that can be reproduced [Kapoor et al., 2024], and prove that AI models do not just perform well in controlled environments, but also in critical/real-world circumstances over time [Ojewale et al., 2024; McIntosh et al., 2024; Chang et al., 2023].
qs.a: Can We Trust AI Benchmarks? An Interdisciplinary Review of Current Issues in AI Evaluation · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: But we do need standardised methods for assessing the trustworthiness of benchmarks from an applied and regulatory perspective.
qs.a: Can We Trust AI Benchmarks? An Interdisciplinary Review of Current Issues in AI Evaluation · Regulators & courts · 2025

elens.an: For the current wave (2026), the recoverable source-level evidence supports the proposition that benchmark scores require contextual assurance and do not alone establish reliable workplace performance. NIST directly recommends comparing evaluation results with similar evaluations, other evidence and existing knowledge, reinforcing the cluster’s distinction between a benchmark result and broader real-world suitability. Material internal variation primarily reflects evidentiary availability rather than disagreement: most supplied excerpts are bibliographies that cite adjacent work on construct validity, contamination, evaluator bias, statistical uncertainty, real-world tasks, productivity and human–AI collaboration, but do not reveal their authors’ own positions or findings. The business-disciplines benchmark excerpt indicates that reproducibility and experimental details exist in supplementary material, yet supplies none of their substance. Accordingly, those sources remain indeterminate and cannot be treated as corroborating, opposing or extending NIST. This assessment applies only to the curated sources and does not indicate the prevalence of this view among 2026 researchers or institutions.

qs.q: Discuss the degree to which evaluation results agree or disagree with similar evaluations or other relevant evidence and existing knowledge.
qs.a: NIST AI 800-2 ipd: Practices for Automated Benchmark Evaluations of Language Models · Regulators & courts · 2026
